Chapter 1 · Topics T4

Rotational (microwave) spectroscopy

9 solved past26 exam-style practice38 new-type questions18 quick-fire

The rigid-rotor chapter is the most heavily examined part of Unit 1: a bond-length calculation, the moment-of-inertia derivation and a level/spectrum sketch appear almost every sitting.

Recap · formulas you need

εJ​=BJ(J+1) cm−1
B=8π2Ich​
I=μr02​,  μ=m1​+m2​m1​m2​​
ΔJ=±1,  line(J→J+1)=2B(J+1)
first line=2B,  spacing=2B
Method
  1. Read the first line (or the spacing): B=line/2.
  2. I=h/(8π2cB) with c in cm s−1.
  3. μ in kg: amu × 1.66×10−27.
  4. r0​=I/μ​, then convert m → Å.
Fig. G9
Fig. G10
Q1-D · Derivation: I = μr₀² (asked ×4)
  1. Let masses m1​,m2​ be at distances r1​,r2​ from the centre of mass C, with r0​=r1​+r2​.
  2. Balance about C: m1​r1​=m2​r2​. Substitute r2​=r0​−r1​: m1​r1​=m2​(r0​−r1​)⇒r1​=m1​+m2​m2​r0​​ and r2​=m1​+m2​m1​r0​​.
  3. I=m1​r12​+m2​r22​=(m1​+m2​)2m1​m22​r02​+m2​m12​r02​​=(m1​+m2​)2m1​m2​(m1​+m2​)r02​​.
  4. ∴ I=m1​+m2​m1​m2​​r02​=μr02​. (Also the energy: Er​=21​Iω2=L2/2I, giving EJ​=8π2Ih2J(J+1)​.)

A · Past ESA questions, fully solved

Q1.1
For a rigid-rotor heteronuclear diatomic molecule AX the first line in the pure rotational spectrum is at 21.18 cm−1. Derive an expression for the moment of inertia and calculate the moment of inertia and bond length of AX. (A = 1.008 amu, X = 35.45 amu; c=3×1010 cm s−1, π=3.14, h=6.627×10−34 J s, 1 amu =1.66×10−27 kg)
Jun-24 · UE23 · Set 26 marks
  1. Derivation: see Q1-D above (I = μr₀²).
  2. First line at 2B, so B=221.18​=10.59 cm−1.
  3. I=8π2cBh​=8(3.14)2(3×1010)(10.59)6.63×10−34​=2.64×10−47 kg m2 (used c=3×1010 cm s−1 because B is in cm−1)
  4. μ=m1​+m2​m1​m2​​=36.461.008×35.45​=0.9801 amu=1.63×10−27 kg.
  5. r0​=I/μ​=1.63×10−272.64×10−47​​=1.27×10−10 m=1.275 A˚.
Answer

I=2.64×10−47 kg m², r0​=1.27 Å

Q1.2
The first line in the pure rotational spectrum of HCl appears at 21.18 cm−1. Calculate the bond length. (H = 1.008, Cl = 35.45 amu; 1 amu =1.66×10−27 kg, c=3×108 m s−1, h=6.6×10−34 J s)
Dec-23 · UE224 marks
  1. Because c is given in m s−1, convert B to m−1 (×100) or use c=3×1010 cm s−1 — same result.
  2. First line at 2B, so B=221.18​=10.59 cm−1.
  3. I=8π2cBh​=8(3.14)2(3×1010)(10.59)6.60×10−34​=2.63×10−47 kg m2 (used c=3×1010 cm s−1 because B is in cm−1)
  4. μ=m1​+m2​m1​m2​​=36.461.008×35.45​=0.9801 amu=1.63×10−27 kg.
  5. r0​=I/μ​=1.63×10−272.63×10−47​​=1.27×10−10 m=1.272 A˚.
Answer

r0​≈1.27 Å

Q1.3
For HBr, the rotational spectrum shows the first line at 17.19 cm−1. Calculate the bond length (rigid rotor). (H = 1.0, Br = 79.9 amu; h=6.627×10−34 J s, c=3×1010 cm s−1)
Jul-23 · UE22 · A4 marks
  1. First line at 2B, so B=217.19​=8.595 cm−1.
  2. I=8π2cBh​=8(3.14)2(3×1010)(8.595)6.63×10−34​=3.26×10−47 kg m2 (used c=3×1010 cm s−1 because B is in cm−1)
  3. μ=m1​+m2​m1​m2​​=80.91.0×79.9​=0.9876 amu=1.64×10−27 kg.
  4. r0​=I/μ​=1.64×10−273.26×10−47​​=1.41×10−10 m=1.409 A˚.
Answer

r0​≈1.41 Å

Q1.4
The first spectral line in the rotational spectrum of HI appears at 13.022 cm−1. Calculate the bond length. (H = 1.0, I = 126.9 amu; c=3×108 m s−1, 1 amu =1.66×10−27 kg, π=3.14, h=6.627×10−34 J s)
Jan-25 · UE24 · Set 13 marks
  1. First line at 2B, so B=213.022​=6.511 cm−1.
  2. I=8π2cBh​=8(3.14)2(3×1010)(6.511)6.63×10−34​=4.30×10−47 kg m2 (used c=3×1010 cm s−1 because B is in cm−1)
  3. μ=m1​+m2​m1​m2​​=127.91.0×126.9​=0.9922 amu=1.65×10−27 kg.
  4. r0​=I/μ​=1.65×10−274.30×10−47​​=1.62×10−10 m=1.616 A˚.

I≈4.30×10−47 kg m², r0​≈1.62 Å

Q1.5
For a rigid-rotor diatomic molecule: (i) draw the energy-level diagram up to J=5; (ii) draw the rotational spectrum; (iii) calculate the moment of inertia and the distance between two spectral lines if B=10.56 cm−1. (c=3×108 m s−1, π=3.14, h=6.625×10−34 J s)
Jun-24 · UE23 · Set 16 marks
  1. (i) Levels εJ​=BJ(J+1): 0, 2B, 6B, 12B, 20B, 30B for J = 0…5 — gaps grow 2B, 4B, 6B, 8B, 10B (Fig. G9).
  2. (ii) Allowed lines J→J+1 at 2B, 4B, 6B, 8B, 10B… equally spaced by 2B; intensity rises then falls (Fig. G10).
  3. (iii) I=8π2cBh​=8(3.14)2(3×1010)(10.56)6.625×10−34​=2.65×10−47 kg m².
  4. Spacing between adjacent lines =2B=2(10.56)=21.12 cm−1.
Answer

I=2.65×10−47 kg m², spacing =21.12 cm−1

Q1.6
For a rotating diatomic molecule: (i) derive an expression for the moment of inertia I; (ii) if B=10 cm−1, give the rotational energy levels for J=0,1,2,3 in cm−1 and draw the energy-level diagram up to J=3.
Jan · UE23A · Set 26 marks
  1. (i) See derivation Q1-D.
  2. (ii) εJ​=10J(J+1): J=0→0; J=1→20; J=2→60; J=3→120 cm−1. Draw four horizontal lines at these heights (gaps 20, 40, 60) with ΔJ=+1 arrows.
Answer

Levels: 0, 20, 60, 120 cm−1

Q1.7
For a rigid-rotor diatomic molecule draw the energy-level diagram up to J=6.
Dec-24 · UE222 marks
  1. εJ​=BJ(J+1): 0, 2B, 6B, 12B, 20B, 30B, 42B — see Fig. G9 (it is drawn to J = 6). Label J on each level and show gaps increasing 2B, 4B, … 12B.
Answer

Levels 0, 2B, 6B, 12B, 20B, 30B, 42B

Q1.8
(ii) If the rotational transition J=0→1 for HCl occurs at 20.68 cm−1, find the energy required for the J=20→21 transition in cm−1. (iii) If the moment of inertia of HBr is 3.26×10−47 kg m², at what wavenumber (in m−1) does the first line appear? (h=6.62×10−34 J s, c=3×108 m s−1)
Jul-23 · UE22 · B6 marks
  1. (ii) J=0→1 gives 2B=20.68, so B=10.34 cm−1. Δε(J→J+1)=2B(J+1); for J=20: 2B×21=21×20.68=434.28 cm−1.
  2. (iii) B=8π2Ich​=8π2(3.26×10−47)(3×108)6.62×10−34​=857.3 m−1 (c in m s−1 gives m−1 directly).
  3. First line =2B=1715 m−1 =17.15 cm−1.
Answer

(ii) 434.28 cm−1 · (iii) ≈ 1715 m−1

Q1.9
For HBr, with bond length 1.404 Å, at what energy (in m−1) does the first line appear in the rotational spectrum? (H = 1.008, Br = 79.9 amu; 1 amu =1.66×10−27 kg, c=3×108 m s−1, h=6.6×10−34 J s)
Jan-25 · UE24 · Set 26 marks
  1. μ=80.9081.008×79.9​ amu=0.9954 amu =1.65×10−27 kg.
  2. I=μr02​=1.65×10−27×(1.404×10−10)2=3.26×10−47 kg m².
  3. B=8π2Ich​=855.4 m−1.
  4. First line =2B=1711 m−1 (≈ 17.11 cm−1).
Answer

First line ≈ 1711 m−1

Q1.Z1.8

Q1.Z1.12

Z2 · Spot the error

Each worked 'solution' contains one mistake.

Q1.Z2.1
Spot the error: HCl first line = 21.18 cm⁻¹, so B = 21.18 cm⁻¹ and I = h/8π²cB.
Q1.Z2.2
Spot the error: I = h/(8π²cB) = 6.63×10⁻³⁴/(8π²·3×10⁸·10.59) = 2.64×10⁻⁴⁷ (c in m s⁻¹, B in cm⁻¹).
Q1.Z2.3
Spot the error: μ of HCl = (1.008×35.45)/(1.008+35.45) = 0.98 kg, so r₀ = √(I/μ).
Q1.Z2.4
Spot the error: Rotational levels J = 0 to 3 for B = 10: 10, 20, 30, 40 cm⁻¹.
Q1.Z2.5
Spot the error: The line J = 20→21 is at 20 × 2B.
Q1.Z2.6
Spot the error: Bond length of HCl is 1.27 m.

N8 · Selection rules and active molecules

Q1.N8.1
Answer

Active (permanent dipole): NO, HBr, OCS, SO₂, H₂O, HD (tiny dipole, weak). Inactive: N₂, CS₂ (linear symmetric), CH₄ (tetrahedral, zero dipole).

Q1.N8.2
Answer

IR needs a dipole change during vibration, which symmetric molecules can still show; rotation of a non-polar molecule produces no oscillating dipole.

Q1.N8.3
Answer

I∝1/B doubles; the first line and the spacing both halve (=2B).

Q1.N8.4
  1. B∝1/I∝1/r02​.
Answer

B falls by a factor of 4; the spectrum compresses by 4.

Q1.N8.5
Answer

Bonds stretch under centrifugal force at high J, so I increases and levels lie slightly below BJ(J+1) (non-rigid rotor). Lines then converge slightly.

Q1.N8.6
  1. Lines at 13.02n; n≤200/13.02=15.4.
Answer

15 lines.

Z1 · True or false

Q1.Z1.1
Answer

False — it appears at 2B (J=0→1).

Q1.Z1.2
Answer

True — 2B(J+2)−2B(J+1)=2B.

Q1.Z1.3
Answer

True — gross selection rule.

Q1.Z1.4
Answer

False — J=0,1,2…; ε0​=0.

Q1.Z1.5
Answer

False — linear and symmetric: no permanent dipole.

Q1.Z1.6
Answer

True — result of the derivation.

Q1.Z1.7
Answer

False — larger μ ⇒ larger I ⇒ smaller B ⇒ lines move lower.

Q1.Z1.8
Answer

True — BJ(J+1)→B(J+1)(J+2) gives 2B(J+1).

Q1.Z1.9
Answer

False — ΔJ = ±1 (±2 is for rotational Raman).

Q1.Z1.10
Answer

False — intensity peaks at Jmax​ (thermal population × degeneracy).

Q1.Z1.11
Answer

False — H₂ has no dipole; HD has a very small one, so only HD is (weakly) active.

Q1.Z1.12
Answer

False — gaps 2B(J+1) increase with J.

Chapter 2 · Topics T5

Vibrational (IR) spectroscopy – harmonic oscillator

8 solved past19 exam-style practice34 new-type questions18 quick-fire4 theory answers

Every paper has a k ↔ ν̄ calculation, usually with zero-point energy, plus the 'why only one line' reason. Learn the one-line formula and practise the unit handling.

Recap · formulas you need

νˉosc​=2πc1​μk​​ cm−1
k=4π2c2νˉ2μ
εv​=(v+21​)νˉosc​
ZPE=ε0​=21​νˉosc​  (E0​=21​hcνˉ)
Δv=±1 ⇒ one line at νˉosc​
Method
  1. Find μ in kg.
  2. νˉ=2πc1​k/μ​ (c in cm s−1 → cm−1).
  3. ZPE =21​νˉ (multiply by hc for joules).
  4. For k: k=4π2c2νˉ2μ.
Fig. G13

A · Past ESA questions, fully solved

Q2.1
(i) The force constant of HF (SHO) is 970 N m−1. Calculate the oscillation frequency (cm−1) and the zero-point energy. (ii) Why does the SHO spectrum show only one line? (c = 3×10⁸ m s⁻¹, π = 3.14, 1 amu = 1.66×10⁻²⁷ kg; H = 1.008, F = 18.99 amu)
Jun-24 · UE23 · Set 16 marks
  1. μ=19.9981.008×18.99​=0.9572 amu =1.59×10−27 kg.
  2. νˉ=2πc1​μk​​=2(3.14)(3×1010)1​1.59×10−27970​​=4147 cm−1.
  3. ZPE =21​νˉ=2074 cm−1 =4.12e−20 J (×hc).
  4. (ii) Levels εv​=(v+21​)νˉ are equally spaced and the selection rule is Δv=±1, so every allowed transition needs the same energy νˉ — one line.
Answer

νˉ≈4147 cm−1, ZPE ≈ 2074 cm−1 ≈ 4.12×10−20 J

Q2.2
Same HF question with H = 1.004 amu, F = 18.998 amu (k = 970 N m⁻¹): (i) oscillation frequency in cm⁻¹; (ii) zero-point energy; (iii) why one line?
Dec-24 · UE226 marks
  1. μ=20.0021.004×18.998​=0.9536 amu =1.58×10−27 kg.
  2. νˉ=2πc1​μk​​=2(3.14)(3×1010)1​1.58×10−27970​​=4155 cm−1.
  3. ZPE =21​νˉ=2077 cm−1 =4.13e−20 J (×hc).
  4. (iii) Equal spacing + Δv=±1.
Answer

νˉ≈4155 cm−1; ZPE ≈ 2077 cm−1

Q2.3
(i) CO absorbs at 2168 cm−1 in a vibrational transition. Calculate the ground-state vibrational energy and force constant (SHO). (c=3×1010 cm s−1, h=6.625×10−34 J s, C = 12, O = 15.999 amu). (ii) Write a note on the failure of the SHO model.

Theory questions · model answers

Why does the SHO spectrum show only one line? (asked ×5)
Levels εv​=(v+21​)νˉ are equally spaced; the selection rule Δv=±1 allows only neighbouring-level jumps. Every jump has the same energy νˉ, so all coincide in one line.
Why is CO₂ IR-active though it has no permanent dipole? (asked ×3)
IR activity needs a change in dipole during vibration, not a permanent dipole. CO₂'s symmetric stretch gives no change (inactive), but the asymmetric stretch and the bending mode do (active). It has no permanent dipole, so it is microwave-inactive.
Why is HI IR-active but H₂ and I₂ inactive?
HI is heteronuclear: stretching changes its dipole moment. H₂ and I₂ are homonuclear: zero dipole at every bond length, so the vibration never changes it.
Write a note on the failure of the SHO model. (asked ×1, relevant ×4)
The SHO assumes a parabolic potential and equal spacing, so it predicts a single line and never dissociation. Real bonds break when stretched (anharmonic, Morse), levels converge, Δv=±2,±3 overtones and hot bands appear, and the molecule can dissociate. The SHO therefore fails at high v and cannot explain overtones.

Q2.Z1.1
Answer

Q2.Z1.2

Q2.Z1.8

Q2.Z1.9

Q2.Z1.10
Answer

Q2.Z1.12

Z2 · Spot the error

Q2.Z2.1
Answer

Q2.Z2.2
Answer

0.95 is in amu; convert to kg (1.58×10⁻²⁷ kg).

Q2.Z2.3
Answer

c = 3×10¹⁰ cm s⁻¹ (or 3×10⁸ m s⁻¹ and then convert m⁻¹ → cm⁻¹ by ÷100).

Q2.Z2.4
Answer

ε₃ = (3 + ½)ν̄ = 3.5ν̄.

Q2.Z2.5
Answer

The reason is equal level spacing with Δv = ±1; overtones are absent in SHO (they appear only in the anharmonic model).

Q2.Z2.6
Answer

IR needs a dipole change; asymmetric stretch and bending change it, so CO₂ is IR-active.

Chapter 3 · Topics T6

Anharmonic oscillator and overtones

5 solved past18 exam-style practice29 new-type questions15 quick-fire

Anharmonic problems are two-equation puzzles: you are given two of fundamental / overtone / ωₑ / xₑ and must find the others. Memorise the three transition expressions.

Recap · formulas you need

εv​=(v+21​)ωˉe​−(v+21​)2ωˉe​xe​
0→1: ωˉe​(1−2xe​)
0→2: 2ωˉe​(1−3xe​)
0→3: 3ωˉe​(1−4xe​)
1→2 (hot): ωˉe​(1−4xe​)
Method
  1. Write the two given transitions as two equations in ωˉe​ and xe​.
  2. Subtract: ωˉe​xe​=f−o/2; then ωˉe​=3f−o and xe​=(f−o/2)/ωˉe​.
  3. If xe​ is given instead: ωˉe​=f/(1−2xe​).
Fig. G15
Fig. G17

A · Past ESA questions, fully solved

Q3.1
For HBr the vibrational spectrum shows the fundamental at 2559.08 cm−1 and the first overtone at 5027.54 cm−1. Calculate the anharmonicity constant (anharmonic model).
Jul-23 · UE22 · A4 marks
  1. Fundamental: ωˉe​(1−2xe​)=2559.08. First overtone: 2ωˉe​(1−3xe​)=5027.54⇒ωˉe​(1−3xe​)=2513.77.
  2. Subtract: ωˉe​xe​=2559.08−2513.77=45.31 cm−1. Then ωˉe​=2559.08+2(45.31)=3(2559.08)−5027.54=2649.70 cm−1.
  3. xe​=45.31/2649.70=0.0171.
Answer

xe​≈0.0171 (ωˉe​≈2649.7 cm−1)

Q3.2
The fundamental stretching frequency of CO is 2143 cm−1 and its anharmonicity constant is 0.01. Calculate its oscillational (equilibrium) frequency.
Jan-25 · UE24 · Set 22 marks
  1. ωˉe​(1−2xe​)=2143.
  2. ωˉe​=1−2(0.01)2143​=0.982143​=2186.7 cm−1.
Answer

ωˉe​≈2186.7 cm−1

Q3.3
Assuming CO shows anharmonic oscillation, calculate the wavenumber of the first overtone if xe​=0.017 and the equilibrium vibrational frequency is 2050 cm−1.
Jul-23 · UE22 · B2 marks
  1. First overtone 0→2: 2ωˉe​(1−3xe​)=2(2050)(1−3×0.017)=2(2050)(0.949).
Answer

3890.9 cm−1

Q3.4
(i) What is the selection rule for the anharmonic oscillator? What is the first overtone transition? Give its expression and explain the terms.
Jan-25 · UE24 · Set 24 marks
  1. Selection rule: Δv=±1,±2,±3… (gross rule: dipole must change).
  2. First overtone v=0→2: Δνˉ=2ωˉe​(1−3xe​), where ωˉe​ is the equilibrium vibrational wavenumber (cm−1) and xe​ is the small positive anharmonicity constant. It is a little less than twice the fundamental.
Answer

2ωˉe​(1−3xe​)

Q3.5
Briefly describe the Born–Oppenheimer approximation and draw the ground and excited electronic states of a diatomic molecule showing rotational and vibrational energy levels (anharmonic model).
Dec-24 · UE235 marks
  1. B–O: electronic, vibrational and rotational energies are independent; E=Erot​+Evib​+Eelec​ (translation negligible), with Erot​≪Evib​≪Eelec​.
  2. Diagram: two Morse curves (ground below, excited above and displaced to longer re​); levels converge towards each dissociation limit; each vibrational level carries closely spaced rotational sub-levels (Fig. G15 for the Morse shape).
Answer

See statement + diagram

Q3.P4.1

Q3.P4.3
Answer

Theory questions · model answers

State the Franck–Condon principle. Draw the three cases and comment on each spectrum. (asked ×5)
Statement: “An electronic transition takes place so rapidly that a vibrating molecule does not change its internuclear distance appreciably during the transition,” so transitions are vertical.
(a) re′​=re′′​: vertical arrow lands on v′=0; the (0,0) line is strongest and intensity falls for (1,0), (2,0)…
(b) re′​>re′′​: arrow lands on a higher v′ (e.g. 2); the (v′,0) line with v′>0 is strongest, so the maximum is displaced along the progression.
(c) re′​≫re′′​: arrow lands above the dissociation limit; a few discrete lines then a continuum (Fig. G21).
The vibrational–electronic spectrum of a molecule shows a continuum. What can be inferred? (asked ×2)
The molecule has been excited above the dissociation limit of the upper state, so it dissociates into atoms. The atoms carry away the excess energy as unquantised kinetic energy, so no discrete lines appear — a continuum. (It also implies re′​≫re′′​.)
State the Born–Oppenheimer approximation. (asked ×3)
The total energy of a molecule is the sum of independent translational, rotational, vibrational and electronic parts; translation is negligible, so E=Erot​+Evib​+Eelec​ with Erot​≪Evib​≪Eelec​ (electronic levels are far apart, rotational levels very close).
What are Rayleigh scattering and Raman scattering? Differentiate Stokes and anti-Stokes lines. (asked ×2)
Rayleigh: elastic scattering — scattered light has the same frequency as the incident light. Raman: inelastic scattering — frequency shifts because the molecule exchanges vibrational/rotational energy with the photon. Stokes: scattered frequency lower than incident (molecule gains energy, goes up). Anti-Stokes: higher than incident (molecule loses energy, comes down); weaker because fewer molecules start in an excited level. (Transcript-based; not on the 2026 slides.)
State the Beer–Lambert law and explain the terms. (older syllabus)
A=log(I0​/I)=εcl: absorbance is proportional to concentration c (mol L⁻¹) and path length l (cm); ε is the molar absorptivity (L mol⁻¹ cm⁻¹); I0​ and I are incident and transmitted intensities. Flag: not on current slides.
Why does the excited electronic state usually have a larger equilibrium bond length?
An electron is promoted to an antibonding orbital (e.g. π→π*), weakening the bond, so the minimum of the upper potential curve shifts to larger r.
Why do homonuclear molecules (H₂, N₂) show vibration/rotation only in electronic spectra?
They have no dipole change for IR or rotation, but all molecules can undergo electronic transitions, which carry vibrational (coarse) and rotational (fine) structure.

N6 · Born–Oppenheimer and energy scales

Q4.N6.1
Answer

E_vib/E_rot ≈ 136; E_elec/E_vib ≈ 28; microwave, IR, UV respectively. Hence E_rot ≪ E_vib ≪ E_elec.

Q4.N6.2
Answer

Since the three energies are independent and additive, ΔE=ΔEelec​+ΔEvib​+ΔErot​: each electronic band splits into vibrational coarse structure, and each vibrational line into rotational fine structure.

Q4.N6.3
Answer

Translational levels are so closely spaced and so small that they are effectively continuous and do not appear in the spectrum.

Q4.N6.4
Answer

Electrons are far lighter than nuclei, so electronic motion is much faster and electronic levels are much farther apart; nuclear motion is slow.

Q4.N6.5
Answer

Only electronic spectroscopy (and Raman); N₂ is inactive in microwave and IR.

N7 · Franck–Condon in words (long answer practice)

Q4.N7.1
Answer

Electronic excitation takes ~10⁻¹⁵ s but nuclei vibrate in ~10⁻¹³ s, so r stays the same during excitation: on a PE-vs-r plot the arrow is vertical.

Q4.N7.2
Answer

For v=0 the probability of finding the nuclei is maximum at the equilibrium position (centre), while for higher v it is at the turning points.

Q4.N7.3
Answer

A series of lines (v′,0) from v′′=0 to successive v′; they converge because the excited-state levels converge (anharmonic), reaching the dissociation limit.

Q4.N7.4
Answer

Coarse = vibrational changes accompanying the electronic transition; fine = rotational changes.

Q4.N7.5
Answer

Franck–Condon overlap of nuclear wave functions governs relative intensity.

True — internuclear distance is unchanged.

Q4.Z1.11
Answer

True — flagged older syllabus.

Q4.Z1.12

False — it depends on polarisability, not permanent dipole.

Chapter 5 · Topics T8–T12

Phase rule, water and Pb–Ag systems

9 solved past35 exam-style practice66 new-type questions18 quick-fire

Phase equilibria questions come in three flavours: derive the rule, count C/P/F for a system, and draw-and-label a diagram. Practise counting until it is automatic.

Recap · formulas you need

F=C−P+2
variables=P(C−1)+2,  constraints=C(P−1)
reduced: F=C−P+1
water: F=3−P
dTdP​=TΔVΔH​
Method
  1. Count phases P (each solid, each immiscible liquid, all gases = 1).
  2. Count components C = species − independent reactions − composition restrictions.
  3. F=C−P+2 (or C−P+1 if pressure is fixed / condensed).
  4. F=2 bivariant, 1 univariant, 0 invariant.
Fig. G22
Fig. G23
Fig. G24
Q5-D · Derivation of the phase rule (asked ×3)
  1. System of C components in P phases at equilibrium. Variables: temperature, pressure and the composition of each phase.
  2. Composition of one phase needs C−1 mole fractions (they sum to 1). For P phases: P(C−1). Add T and P: total variables =P(C−1)+2.
  3. At equilibrium the chemical potential of each component is equal in every phase: μiα​=μiβ​=μiγ​=⋯ — that is (P−1) equations per component, C(P−1) constraints in all.
  4. F= variables − constraints =P(C−1)+2−C(P−1)=PC−P+2−CP+C= C−P+2.

A · Past ESA questions, fully solved

Derive the phase rule for a system of C components and P phases in equilibrium.

  1. See derivation Q5-D.
Answer

F=C−P+2

Q5.2

Q5.3
(i) Define component. Give the number of phases and components for the closed system MgCO3​(s) ⇌ MgO(s) + CO2​(g). (ii) Define eutectoid and peritectic points in the Fe–C system.
Jan · UE23A · Set 24 marks
  1. (i) Component: the smallest number of independently variable constituents by which the composition of every phase can be expressed. Phases: MgCO₃(s), MgO(s), CO₂(g): P=3. Species 3 − 1 reaction = C=2 (e.g. choose MgO and CO₂: MgCO₃ = MgO + CO₂).
  2. (ii) Eutectoid: one solid phase transforms isothermally into two other solids (austenite → ferrite + cementite, 727 °C, 0.76 wt% C). Peritectic: liquid + one solid → a new solid (liquid + δ-ferrite → austenite, 1493 °C, 0.17 wt% C). Flag: Fe–C is not in the current material; values are standard textbook figures.
Answer

P=3, C=2

Q5.4
(i) Why is the phase rule F=C−P+2 for water but F=C−P+1 for the Pb–Ag system? (ii) For CaCO3​(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO2​(g) in a closed container give the number of components and phases.
Jan-25 · UE24 · Set 26 marks
  1. (i) Water is a one-component system with T and P both variable. For Pb–Ag, C=2 so F=4−P, giving F=3 for one phase — a 3-D diagram. Pressure is therefore fixed (≈1 atm) and, since solid–liquid equilibria (condensed systems, no gas) hardly depend on pressure, the rule reduces to F=C−P+1.
  2. (ii) P=3 (CaCO₃, CaO, CO₂); species 3 − 1 reaction ⇒ C=2.
Answer

(ii) P=3, C=2

Q5.5
(i) Draw a neat labelled phase diagram of water (areas, lines, triple point, critical point, pressure, temperature) and calculate the degree of freedom along the freezing-point curve. (ii) What is the condensed phase rule and why is it applied to the two-component Pb–Ag system?
Jan-25 · UE24 · Set 16 marks
  1. (i) Diagram: Fig. G22. Triple point O: 0.0098 °C, 4.58 mmHg; critical point A: 374 °C, 218 atm. Along a curve C=1,P=2: F=1−2+2=1 (univariant).
  2. (ii) F=C−P+1: used when pressure is constant and the gas phase is absent (condensed systems), as in Pb–Ag where P has little effect.
Answer

F=1 on the freezing curve

Q5.6
(i) Draw a neat labelled phase diagram of the water system with areas, lines and T, P values at the triple and critical points. (ii) Which phases are in equilibrium on the metastable curve? (iii) Calculate F at the triple point.
Jun-24 · UE23 · Set 26 marks
  1. (i) Fig. G22.
  2. (ii) Supercooled liquid water ⇌ vapour (curve OA′, an extension of OA below the triple point).
  3. (iii) C=1,P=3: F=1−3+2=0 — invariant.
Answer

(ii) liquid + vapour; (iii) F = 0

Q5.7
(i) Draw the phase diagram of water, label areas and boundaries, and calculate F in the areas, along phase boundaries and at the triple point. (ii) Using the Clausius–Clapeyron equation, discuss why the melting-point curve has a negative slope. (iii) What is the reduced phase rule and when is it used?
Dec-24 · UE238 marks
  1. (i) Fig. G22: areas F=3−1=2; lines F=3−2=1; triple point F=3−3=0.
  2. (ii) dTdP​=TΔVΔHfus​​. Fusion: ΔH>0; ice → water decreases volume (ΔV<0), so dP/dT<0: raising pressure lowers the melting point. The slope is steep because ∣ΔV∣ is small. (OA and OB have ΔV>0 and large, so gentle positive slopes.)
  3. (iii) F=C−P+1 — for condensed systems at constant pressure.
Answer

F = 2, 1, 0; dP/dT < 0 because ΔV < 0

Q5.8
(i) Draw a neat labelled phase diagram of the lead–silver system indicating areas and lines. Give the temperature and composition at the eutectic point. (ii) For the Fe–C system mention the phases in equilibrium, temperature and wt% C at the peritectic point.
Jun-24 · UE23 · Set 16 marks
  1. (i) Fig. G23: Pb melts at 327 °C, Ag at 961 °C; curves AO and BO fall to the eutectic point O at 303 °C, 2.6 % Ag (97.4 % Pb); areas: liquid melt; liquid + solid Ag; liquid + solid Pb; solid Pb + solid Ag. At O: C=2,P=3,F=0.
  2. (ii) Peritectic: liquid + δ-ferrite ⇌ austenite at 1493 °C, 0.17 wt% C (flag: Fe–C not in current material).
Answer

Eutectic: 303 °C, 2.6 % Ag

Q5.9
(i) Draw a neat labelled phase diagram of the CO2​ system with areas, lines, triple and critical points (T, P). (ii) What is the reduced phase rule? Why is the general Gibbs rule not applied to a two-component system?
Jan · UE23A · Set 26 marksNot on current slides
  1. (i) Like water but the solid–liquid line leans right (positive slope, since solid CO₂ is denser). Triple point −56.6 °C, 5.11 atm; critical point 31.1 °C, 73 atm; at 1 atm CO₂ sublimes (−78.5 °C). Flag: not in current material; standard values.
  2. (ii) For C=2, F=4−P gives F=3 when P=1, needing three axes (T,P, composition). So pressure is fixed: F=C−P+1.
Answer

Triple −56.6 °C / 5.11 atm; critical 31.1 °C / 73 atm

E · Answer key for sections B, C and D

Set 1 · Count P, C and F

Q5.P1.1
  1. single substance, three physical phases.
Answer

P=3, C=1, F=1−3+2=0 (invariant)

Q5.P1.2
  1. one substance.
Answer

P=2, C=1, F=1−2+2=1 (univariant)

Q5.P1.3
  1. 3 species − 1 reaction.
Answer

P=3, C=2, F=2−3+2=1 (univariant)

Q5.P1.4
  1. 3 species − 1 reaction.
Answer

P=3, C=2, F=2−3+2=1 (univariant)

Q5.P1.5
  1. gas has NH₃ : HCl = 1 : 1, an extra restriction.
Answer

P=2, C=1, F=1−2+2=1 (univariant)

Q5.P1.6
  1. the 1 : 1 restriction is lost.
Answer

P=2, C=2, F=2−2+2=2 (bivariant)

Q5.P1.7
  1. NaCl and water; solid, solution, vapour.
Answer

P=3, C=2, F=2−3+2=1 (univariant)

Q5.P1.8
  1. two components; liquid, liquid, vapour.
Answer

P=3, C=2, F=2−3+2=1 (univariant)

Q5.P1.9
  1. one component, three phases.
Answer

P=3, C=1, F=1−3+2=0 (invariant)

Q5.P1.10
  1. single gas phase; composition fixed by [PCl₃] = [Cl₂].
Answer

P=1, C=1, F=1−1+2=2 (bivariant)

Q5.P1.11
  1. 3 species − 1 reaction.
Answer

P=1, C=2, F=2−1+2=3 (multivariant)

Q5.P1.12
  1. salt and water as components; hydrate, anhydrate, vapour.
Answer

P=3, C=2, F=2−3+2=1 (univariant)

Set 2 · Number of variables and constraints (derivation check)

Q5.P2.1
  1. Variables =P(C−1)+2; constraints =C(P−1).
Answer

Composition: 1; total variables: 3; constraints: 0; F=3−0=3

Q5.P2.2
  1. Variables =P(C−1)+2; constraints =C(P−1).
Answer

Composition: 2; total variables: 4; constraints: 2; F=4−2=2

Q5.P2.3
  1. Variables =P(C−1)+2; constraints =C(P−1).
Answer

Composition: 3; total variables: 5; constraints: 4; F=5−4=1

Q5.P2.4
  1. Variables =P(C−1)+2; constraints =C(P−1).
Answer

Composition: 4; total variables: 6; constraints: 3; F=6−3=3

Q5.P2.5
  1. Variables =P(C−1)+2; constraints =C(P−1).
Answer

Composition: 8; total variables: 10; constraints: 9; F=10−9=1

Set 3 · Water diagram

Q5.P3.1
  1. F=3−P.
Answer

Area F=2 (bivariant); line F=1 (univariant); triple point F=0 (invariant).

Q5.P3.2
Answer

OA vaporisation (water ⇌ vapour); OB sublimation (ice ⇌ vapour); OC fusion (ice ⇌ water, negative slope); OA′ metastable supercooled water ⇌ vapour.

Q5.P3.3
Answer

Triple point 0.0098 °C, 4.58 mmHg; critical point 374 °C, 218 atm.

Q5.P3.4
Answer

The liquid–vapour interface vanishes — above the critical temperature no pressure can liquefy the vapour.

Q5.P3.5
Answer

It decreases: ice melts to a smaller volume (ΔV<0), so by Clausius–Clapeyron dP/dT<0.

Q5.P3.6
Answer

P=2, F=1; at fixed 1 atm T is fixed at 0 °C (normal melting point).

Set 4 · Clausius–Clapeyron slopes (extension)

Q5.P4.1
  1. dP/dT=ΔH/(TΔV).
Answer

dP/dT=−1.35×107 Pa K−1≈−133 atm K−1 — large and negative: very steep curve OC.

Q5.P4.2
  1. Same equation.
Answer

dP/dT≈3567 Pa K−1 ≈ 35.2×10⁻³ atm K⁻¹ — positive and tiny by comparison (large ΔV), so OA is gentle.

Q5.P4.3
Answer

ΔV>0⇒dP/dT>0: melting curve leans right (e.g. CO₂).

Set 5 · Reduced phase rule and the Pb–Ag system

Q5.P5.1
  1. Condensed system (no gas), pressure fixed.
Answer

Because C=2 would need 3-D at F=C−P+2; at constant pressure one variable is removed.

Q5.P5.2
  1. C=2,P=3.
Answer

F=2−3+1=0 (invariant). Phases: solid Pb, solid Ag and liquid melt (303 °C, 2.6 % Ag).

Q5.P5.3
Answer

Curves: P=2 so F=1 (univariant); liquid region P=1 so F=2 (bivariant).

Q5.P5.4
  1. 10 % Ag is richer in Ag than the eutectic (2.6 % Ag), so the melt cools until it meets the Ag freezing-point curve (O to the Ag melting point): solid Ag separates first and the melt becomes richer in Pb.
Answer

Solid Ag separates first on the Ag-side curve; the melt composition slides down that curve to O (303 °C, 2.6 % Ag); there Pb and Ag crystallise together at constant temperature (halt, F = 0); below 303 °C: solid Pb + solid Ag. (A melt with less than 2.6 % Ag would separate Pb first.)

Q5.P5.5
Answer

A mixture of two components with the lowest freezing point of all compositions; it has a definite composition and a sharp melting point and solidifies at constant temperature (F = 0).

Q5.P5.6
Answer

At the eutectic F=0: temperature stays fixed while all three phases coexist until solidification is complete.

Set 6 · Cooling curves (thermal analysis)

Q5.P6.1
Answer

Smooth fall, then a halt at the freezing point (solid and liquid coexist, F=C−P+1=1−2+1=0), then a fall again. (Fig. G24)

Q5.P6.2
Answer

Fall → break (change of slope) when the first solid appears (heat of crystallisation slows cooling, F=1) → fall → halt at the eutectic temperature (F=0) → fall.

Q5.P6.3
Answer

Record cooling curves for several compositions; read the break and halt temperatures; plot them against composition and join the break points (liquidus) and the common halt temperature (eutectic line).

N2 · Complete the F-table

Q5.N2.1
  1. C=1.
Answer

Areas: P=1, F=2. OA, OB, OC: P=2, F=1. OA′ (metastable, liquid+vapour): P=2, F=1. Triple point O: P=3, F=0. Critical point A: liquid and vapour become identical; treated as invariant (F=0).

Q5.N2.2
  1. C=2, reduced rule.
Answer

Liquid melt: P=1, F=2. Liquid + one solid: P=2, F=1. Solid Pb + solid Ag: P=2, F=1. Curves AO and BO: P=2, F=1. Eutectic O: P=3 (Pb + Ag + melt), F=0. Pure metal melting point A or B: C=1, P=2 ⇒ F = 1−2+1 = 0.

Q5.N2.3
  1. F=0.
Answer

F = 0 (invariant): T and P are both fixed; changing either removes at least one phase.

Q5.N2.4
  1. Two phases, C=1.
Answer

F = 1 − 2 + 2 = 1; fixing the pressure at 1 atm uses up the single degree of freedom, so T is fixed at 100 °C.

Q5.N2.5
  1. F≥0⇒P≤C+2.
Answer

P_max = C + 2 = 5 (general rule); for a condensed system, P_max = C + 1.

Q5.N2.6
  1. Pmax​=C+2 and C+1.
Answer

General: 3, 4, 5, 6. Condensed: 2, 3, 4, 5 (so Pb–Ag has at most 3 phases at the eutectic).

N6 · Interpret cooling curves

Q5.N6.1
  1. Reduced rule, C=1.
Answer

Solid + liquid in equilibrium: F = 1 − 2 + 1 = 0 — temperature stays constant until all liquid solidifies.

Q5.N6.2
Answer

Break at 800 °C = start of crystallisation of the first solid (F=1, cooling slows); halt at 303 °C = eutectic crystallisation, three phases, F=0.

Q5.N6.3
Answer

The eutectic composition, 2.6 % Ag (97.4 % Pb).

Q5.N6.4
Answer

(i) 2.6 % (halt at 303 °C) and the pure metals (halt at 327 °C for 0 %, 961 °C for 100 %); (ii) 50 %; (iii) 100 % Ag.

Q5.N6.5
Answer

It is longest at the eutectic composition (all liquid solidifies there) and decreases towards the pure-metal ends (little eutectic liquid).

Q5.N6.6
Answer

Plot break temperatures against composition for the liquidus curves, the common halt temperature for the eutectic line, and the pure-metal halts for the two ends (see Fig. G24).

N7 · Definitions in your own words

Q5.N7.1
Answer

Homogeneous, physically distinct, mechanically separable part. Examples: a mixture of gases is one phase; two immiscible liquids (oil + water) are two phases; each polymorph (rhombic/monoclinic sulphur) is a separate phase.

Q5.N7.2
Answer

Smallest number of independently variable constituents that express every phase's composition. Zero/negative coefficients let a constituent be absent from a phase or be consumed (e.g. CaO = CaCO₃ − CO₂).

Q5.N7.3
Answer

Number of intensive variables (T, P, concentration) that can be varied independently without changing the number of phases; for liquid water alone F = 2.

Q5.N7.4
Answer

A system in which the gas phase is absent, so small pressure changes have little effect (solid–liquid).

Q5.N7.5
Answer

A state not at the true minimum of Gibbs energy but persisting until disturbed — supercooled water below 0 °C (curve OA′).

Q5.N7.6
Answer

Heterogeneous system at equilibrium, not influenced by external forces (gravity, electrical, magnetic).

Q5.N7.7
Answer

F = 2, 1, 0 respectively.

N8 · Derivation variants and logic

Q5.N8.1
Answer

Pressure is held constant (condensed system), removing one variable: F=C−P+2−1=C−P+1.

Q5.N8.2
Answer

F=2−1+2=3: T, P and composition must all be specified — a 3-D diagram.

Q5.N8.3
Answer

In each phase the mole fractions sum to 1, so only C−1 are independent.

Q5.N8.4
Answer

For each of C components, P chemical potentials must be equal: P−1 independent equations.

Q5.N8.5
Answer

variables =2(2)+2=6; constraints =3; F=3 (=3−2+2).

Q5.N8.6
Answer

Matter flows from higher to lower μ; at equilibrium μ is equal in all phases and there is no net transfer.

Z1 · True or false

Q5.Z1.1
Answer

False — at constant pressure use F=C−P+1.

Q5.Z1.2
Answer

True — a phase is not defined by the number of pieces.

Q5.Z1.3
Answer

True — NH₃ : HCl = 1 : 1 in the gas, so one component; C=2 if extra NH₃ or HCl is added.

Q5.Z1.4
Answer

False — F = 1 − 3 + 2 = 0.

Q5.Z1.5
Answer

False — negative: ΔV<0.

Q5.Z1.6
Answer

False — it lowers it slightly.

Q5.Z1.7
Answer

True — 374 °C, 218 atm.

Q5.Z1.8
Answer

True — solid Pb, solid Ag and melt.

Q5.Z1.9
Answer

False — the lowest.

Q5.Z1.10
Answer

False — its vapour pressure is higher.

Q5.Z1.11
Answer

False — components are the minimum independent set; species − reactions − restrictions.

Q5.Z1.12
Answer

True — gases are completely miscible.

Z2 · Spot the error

Q5.Z2.1
Answer

Three species minus one reaction gives C = 2.

Q5.Z2.2
Answer

F = C − P + 2 with C = 1: 1 − 3 + 2 = 0.

Q5.Z2.3
Answer

Variables = P(C − 1) + 2 (mole fractions sum to 1).

Q5.Z2.4
Answer

Use the reduced rule: 2 − 3 + 1 = 0.

Q5.Z2.5
Answer

Ice is less dense (ΔV < 0 on melting), so the slope is negative.

Q5.Z2.6
Answer

F = 1 − 2 + 2 = 1.

A · Past ESA questions, fully solved

Q6.1
(i) What is computational chemistry? Give any three applications of computational chemistry.
Jan-25 · UE24 · Set 27 marks
  1. Definition: a set of techniques that solves chemical problems by simulating molecular, biological or materials systems to give reliable, accurate, atomic-level information, using theoretical chemistry built into efficient computer programs.
  2. Three applications: (1) predicting molecular properties — HOMO/LUMO and UV-Vis, IR, NMR spectra; (2) studying reaction mechanisms and kinetics; (3) designing new materials (conductivity, thermal stability); (also drug discovery by simulating drug–target interaction).
Answer

Definition + any three applications

E · Answer key for sections B, C and D

Set 1 · Short answers

Q6.P1.1
Answer

Techniques to simulate chemical systems and compute properties at the atomic level. First theoretical work: Heitler and London, 1927.

Q6.P1.2
Answer

Molecular properties/spectra, reaction mechanism and kinetics, material design, drug discovery.

Q6.P1.3
Answer

Classical (molecular mechanics, molecular dynamics): Newtonian, atoms as spheres and bonds as springs, electrons ignored, very fast. Quantum (semi-empirical, ab initio, DFT): based on the Schrödinger equation, treat electrons explicitly, slower but more accurate.

Q6.P1.4
Answer

Model of a molecule as balls (atoms) joined by springs (bonds), energy from classical force fields; large molecules such as steroids can be optimised in seconds.

Q6.P1.5
Answer

DFT derives the electron density directly instead of a conventional many-electron wave function; faster than ab initio but slower than semi-empirical.

Q6.P1.6
Answer

Speed: MM > semi-empirical > DFT > ab initio. Accuracy (generally): ab initio > DFT > semi-empirical > MM.

Q6.P1.7
Answer

Easier, cheaper and safer than experiments. It does not replace experiments; it helps chemists design and develop desired products.

Q6.P1.8
Answer

1 Define geometry of C₂H₄; 2 select a basis set; 3 apply the method to get orbital energies and density; 4 solve the equations for the wave function / electron density; 5 visualise the orbitals (HOMO = π, LUMO = π*).

Q6.P1.9
Answer

Each carbon is sp²: 2 C–H σ bonds + 1 C–C σ bond; one unhybridised p orbital per carbon forms the π bond. HOMO = π, LUMO = π*.

Q6.P1.10
Answer

Scopes: accelerated molecular discovery; property prediction; reaction-pathway mapping; structure generation. Advantages: massive speed-up (hours/days → milliseconds once trained); large-scale screening; pattern recognition of structure–property relations.

N1 · Which method would you use?

Q6.N1.1
Answer

Molecular mechanics — balls and springs, very fast.

Q6.N1.2
Answer

Molecular dynamics — applies laws of motion to follow atom movements.

Q6.N1.3
Answer

Semi-empirical — a middle road; can handle transition states and excited states.

Q6.N1.4
Answer

DFT — derives electron density directly; faster than ab initio, slower than semi-empirical.

Q6.N1.5
Answer

Ab initio — based on the Schrödinger equation and the wave function; the most demanding.

Q6.N1.6
Answer

A quantum method (DFT or semi-empirical).

Q6.N1.7
Answer

Fast classical methods (MM/MD) plus AI/ML surrogate models trained on quantum data.

Q6.N1.8
Answer

MD for dynamics, DFT for electronic structure; AI to speed up screening.

N2 · Compare the methods

Q6.N2.1
Answer

MM: classical, no electrons, fastest, lowest. MD: classical dynamics, no electrons, fast. Semi-empirical: quantum (approximate Schrödinger), yes, fast, medium. DFT: quantum (density), yes, medium, high. Ab initio: quantum (wave function), yes, slowest, highest.

Q6.N2.2
Answer

The set of equations/parameters that gives the potential energy of a molecule as the sum of attractive and repulsive atom–atom interactions (bond stretching, bending, non-bonded).

Q6.N2.3
Answer

A mathematical function from the Schrödinger equation describing electrons; ∣ψ∣2 gives the electron probability density.

Q6.N2.4
Answer

The set of mathematical functions used to build molecular orbitals in a calculation (step 2 of the ethylene workflow).

Q6.N2.5
Answer

Cost grows quickly with molecular size and accuracy; results depend on the chosen method/basis set and are not a replacement for experiment.

Q6.N2.6
Answer

Walter Kohn and John Pople (DFT and computational methods). [Added for clarity; 2013: Karplus, Levitt, Warshel.]

N3 · Ethylene and the electronic-structure workflow

Q6.N3.1
Answer

5 σ (4 C–H + 1 C–C) and 1 π; each carbon is sp².

Q6.N3.2
Answer

π: in-phase overlap of the two p orbitals (bonding, HOMO). π*: out-of-phase overlap with a node between the carbons (antibonding, LUMO).

Q6.N3.3
Answer

1 Define geometry. 2 Select basis set. 3 Apply the method (orbital energies and density). 4 Solve equations (wave function / density). 5 Visualise (orbital diagrams, density maps, HOMO and LUMO).

Q6.N3.4
Answer

Absorption of light promotes an electron HOMO → LUMO; a smaller gap absorbs at longer wavelength (see Ch. 4 N1).

Q6.N3.5
Answer

Its π electrons are higher in energy and more exposed than the σ framework; the HOMO (π) donates and the LUMO (π*) accepts electrons.

Q6.N3.6
Answer

It is described by torsional terms in a force field: staggered conformers lowest, eclipsed highest (Fig. G25).

N4 · AI-enhanced computational chemistry

Q6.N4.1
Answer

Quantum simulations generate data → build a dataset → train an ML model → predict properties in milliseconds.

Q6.N4.2
Answer

Accelerated molecular discovery; property prediction; reaction-pathway mapping; structure generation.

Q6.N4.3
Answer

Massive speed-up (hours/days → milliseconds after training); broad screening of vast chemical spaces; pattern recognition of subtle structure–property relationships.

Q6.N4.4
Answer

It is trained on data produced by quantum simulations (or experiments); the model interpolates, it does not replace the underlying physics.

Q6.N4.5
Answer

Battery-electrolyte or polymer screening: predict stability and conductivity of thousands of candidates before synthesis.

Z1 · True or false

Q6.Z1.1
Answer

True — classical force field.

Q6.Z1.2
Answer

False — it derives the electron density directly.

Q6.Z1.3
Answer

False — slower but more accurate.

Q6.Z1.4
Answer

False — it complements them.

Q6.Z1.5
Answer

True — slide 3.

Q6.Z1.6
Answer

True — slide 16.

Q6.Z1.7
Answer

False — classical methods ignore electrons.

Q6.Z1.8
Answer

True — slide 20.

Q6.Z1.9
Answer

True — slide 10.

Q6.Z1.10
Answer

True — slide 9.

Z2 · Spot the error

Q6.Z2.1
Answer

Ab initio ('from the beginning') uses the Schrödinger equation with no empirical parameters (that is what semi-empirical methods add).

Q6.Z2.2
Answer

DFT is faster than ab initio but slower than semi-empirical.

Q6.Z2.3
Answer

HOMO is π (bonding); LUMO is π*.
